description:
GATRIX is a team of five innovators from Bangladesh. Our project, TerraScope, uses NASA satellite data and AI to monitor environmental changes.

Exploring Earth, Empowering Tomorrow.
summary:
Team GATRIX developed **TerraScope**, an interactive Earth observation dashboard for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It helps users investigate where and when vegetation greenness has changed using NASA Earth observation data.

Using NASA Terra MODIS observations accessed through AppEEARS, TerraScope enables users to explore vegetation trends from 2001 to 2024 across representative study points in Bangladesh, Assam, Chiang Mai, and Riyadh.

Our Sundarbans pilot compares month-matched observations from 2001–2005 and 2020–2024 using MODIS data. A separate 10-meter Copernicus Sentinel-2 comparison allows users to explore January 2020 and January 2024 imagery through an interactive slider, inspect pixel-level vegetation measurements, and download GeoTIFF comparison layers.

TerraScope addresses the **“Be An Earth System Trend Detective!”** challenge by connecting interactive satellite maps with measurable vegetation trends. By presenting observation coverage, data quality considerations, and trend uncertainty, the platform helps students, educators, and researchers investigate environmental change while understanding the limitations of satellite observations.

Our goal is to make Earth observation data more accessible, interactive, and scientifically transparent.
details:
TerraScope — The Vegetation Trend Detective

TerraScope is an interactive web dashboard that helps students, educators, and curious explorers investigate how vegetation greenness changes over time. We started with Bangladesh and added representative study points in Assam, Chiang Mai, and Riyadh so users can explore vegetation patterns across different climates and landscapes.

The dashboard uses NASA Terra MODIS observations accessed through AppEEARS to show NDVI and EVI from 2001 to 2024. Users can select a study point, time period, and vegetation index, then explore long-term trends, seasonal patterns, and observation coverage. NASA GIBS imagery helps users locate each study point on the map, and NASA POWER provides monthly temperature and precipitation as climate context.

In the Sundarbans, users can drag a before-and-after slider to compare January 2020 and January 2024 using 10-meter Copernicus Sentinel-2 imagery. They can switch from true-color imagery to measured NDVI, click a pixel to see its values for both periods, and download the comparison layers as GeoTIFFs. A separate MODIS view compares 2001–2005 with 2020–2024 using the same calendar months in both periods to reduce seasonal differences.

Our creative approach is to connect what users see on a satellite image with what they can measure at the same location. We considered cloud screening, missing observations, differences in spatial resolution, and seasonal effects. The dashboard reports data coverage and trend uncertainty so users can judge how much evidence supports a finding. The Sundarbans comparison covers a pilot area, and the measured NDVI changes describe vegetation greenness within that area.

We built the dashboard with Next.js, React, and TypeScript, using MapLibre GL JS for interactive maps and Recharts for charts. We used Python, NumPy, and Rasterio to process satellite imagery and prepare the comparison layers. Our goal is to make Earth observation data easier to explore and give users a practical way to ask where vegetation is changing, when it changed, and how confidently they can interpret the result.
